About This Part
Volume 11B converts the observability requirements from Part A into an operational Prometheus monitoring
platform. The part progresses from architecture and metric exposition through discovery, exporters, PromQL,
recording rules, alert design, Alertmanager routing, high availability, and a production-style capstone. Prometheus is treated as a reliability system rather than a graphing utility. Every chapter therefore connects
collection behavior, query semantics, failure modes, resource consumption, security boundaries, ownership,
testing, and operational evidence. Volume 11 Roadmap

Scope, Safety and Cost Controls

Run scrape-failure, alert-routing, load, cardinality, retention, network, and high-availability tests only in
disposable or explicitly approved environments.

Use synthetic targets, labels, credentials, notifications, and incident channels. Never use production paging
routes for learning exercises.

Define retention, storage capacity, sample limits, label limits, target limits, query limits, and cleanup before
generating telemetry at scale.

Treat metric labels and annotations as potentially sensitive data. Do not expose secrets, personal
identifiers, tokens, full URLs with credentials, or customer-controlled free text.

Validate configuration and rules before reload.









VOLUME 11B | CHAPTER 11
Chapter 11: Prometheus Architecture and Deployment
Fundamentals
Designing the collection, storage, query, rule and alerting control plane
Learning Objectives

Explain the Prometheus server data path from discovery and scraping to TSDB, rules, queries and
notifications.

Distinguish single-server, high-availability pair, federation and remote-storage architectures.

Plan retention, capacity, persistence, resource requests, backups, security and failure boundaries.

Validate configuration, health, readiness, target state, runtime state and self-monitoring.

Create a reversible local deployment suitable for the remaining labs. Core Concepts
Pull-based collection
Prometheus normally discovers or receives a list of targets and periodically scrapes their HTTP metric
endpoints. A successful scrape produces timestamped samples plus internal scrape health metrics. Pulling
makes target liveness, scrape duration, sample count, and errors visible to the collector. Local time-series database
The server stores recent samples in its local time-series database. Operational design must account for write-
ahead logging, block compaction, retention, disk growth, I/O, memory, restart behavior, and the fact that local
storage is not a general backup system. Rules and alert delivery
The rule manager evaluates recording and alerting rules at configured intervals. Alerting rules produce labeled
alert instances; Prometheus sends them to every configured Alertmanager endpoint. Alertmanager then
groups, routes, inhibits, silences, and notifies.

alerting rules at configured intervals. Alerting rules produce labeled
alert instances; Prometheus sends them to every configured Alertmanager endpoint. Alertmanager then
groups, routes, inhibits, silences, and notifies. Reference Architecture
[Targets / Exporters] --HTTP scrape--> [Prometheus A] --alerts--> [Alertmanager A]
| | \ <mesh>
+-----------------------------> [Prometheus B] --alerts--> [Alertmanager B]

Architecture Rule An HA pair improves availability but does not automatically create durable long-term
storage or consistent global querying. Treat availability, durability and global-view requirements as separate
design decisions. Deployment Baseline

Hands-On Lab
1. Create a lab directory with configuration, rules, data and evidence subdirectories.
2. Run Prometheus using a pinned local container image or approved binary.
3. Validate configuration before startup.
4. Query health and readiness endpoints, then inspect runtime and build information.
5. Scrape Prometheus itself and confirm up, scrape duration and sample metrics.

6. Restart the server and confirm persistence.
7. Introduce one invalid configuration change, prove the validator rejects it, and restore the known-good file.
8. Record disk usage and core self-metrics before cleanup. Validation Evidence

Validated configuration output.

Screenshot or API output showing the self-target is up.

PromQL results for up and selected prometheus_* metrics.

Restart evidence showing retained data.

Failure-and-recovery log for the rejected configuration.

Sanitized architecture diagram and capacity assumptions. Interview Questions and Model Answers
Q: Why does Prometheus commonly use pull-based scraping?
A: It centralizes scrape scheduling and makes target availability, scrape latency and scrape errors observable
while allowing the server to control collection cadence. Q: Does two Prometheus replicas guarantee durable storage?
A: No. Replicas improve collector availability. Durability and long-term retention require separate storage and
recovery design. Q: What should be validated before a reload?
A: The main configuration, included scrape files, all rule files, secrets or mounted paths, target changes, and
the rollback procedure. Chapter Summary

Prometheus combines discovery, scraping, local TSDB storage, PromQL, rule evaluation and alert
forwarding.

Availability, durability, retention and global querying are separate architecture concerns.

Self-monitoring and safe configuration reloads are mandatory production capabilities.

Naming and Labels

Use a stable application or subsystem prefix when it improves ownership and collision avoidance.

Use base units such as seconds and bytes; include the unit in the metric name.

Counters normally use the _total suffix.

Labels should represent bounded dimensions that users will aggregate, filter or route on.

Do not use request IDs, email addresses, usernames, raw paths, full error messages, timestamps, random
values or unbounded customer input as labels.

Keep one metric name semantically consistent across every target that exposes it.

Illustrative Python instrumentation
from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, Gauge, start_http_server
REQUESTS = Counter(
"checkout_http_requests_total",
"Completed HTTP requests",
["method", "route", "status_class"],
)
LATENCY = Histogram(
"checkout_http_request_duration_seconds",
"HTTP request latency",
["method", "route"],
buckets=(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5),
)
INFLIGHT = Gauge("checkout_http_requests_in_flight", "In-flight HTTP requests")
start_http_server(8000)
Cardinality Budget Estimate series before deployment: metric families × unique label combinations ×
targets. Test the worst realistic label set, not only a happy-path sample.

Hands-On Lab
1. Build a small HTTP service with request count, latency and in-flight metrics.
2. Use route templates and status classes as bounded labels.
3. Generate successful, failing, fast and slow synthetic requests.
4. Scrape the service and inspect raw exposition.
5. Write PromQL to calculate request rate, error ratio and mean duration.
6. Add a deliberately unsafe request_id label in a disposable branch, measure series growth, then remove it.
7. Restart the service and explain the counter-reset behavior.
8. Document the final metric contract.

Validation Evidence

Source code and dependency manifest.

Raw /metrics sample with HELP and TYPE lines.







Restart test showing correct rate handling. Interview Questions and Model Answers
Q: Why are raw URLs dangerous labels?
A: Dynamic path segments create unbounded label values and therefore an uncontrolled number of time series. Use normalized route templates. Q: When should a histogram be preferred over a summary?
A: When server-side aggregation across instances and configurable bucket-based SLO analysis are required. Q: How do you calculate average latency from a histogram?
A: Divide the rate of the _sum series by the rate of the _count series over the same range, grouped by the same
dimensions. Chapter Summary

Metric type is defined by behavior, not by the desired chart shape.

Bounded labels and stable naming are essential for correctness and cost control.

Instrumentation must be validated under errors, concurrency, restarts and worst-case label combinations.

Chapter 13: Service Discovery, Scrape Configuration and
Relabeling
Controlling which targets and samples enter the monitoring system
Learning Objectives

Build global and per-job scrape settings with appropriate intervals and timeouts.

Use static targets and understand the role of dynamic service-discovery mechanisms.

Apply target relabeling, metric relabeling and alert relabeling at the correct stage.

Normalize ownership, environment and service labels without creating conflicts.

Debug discovery, dropped targets, scrape failures, duplicate series and sample limits. Scrape Lifecycle
service discovery
-> discovered labels (__meta_*)
-> target relabeling
-> final target labels and scrape address/path/scheme
-> HTTP scrape
-> metric relabeling
-> ingestion into TSDB
-> rule evaluation
-> alert relabeling before Alertmanager

scrape_timeout: 10s

Hands-On Lab
1. Add two static application targets and one node exporter target.
2. Assign service, team and environment labels.
3. Create one target relabel rule that retains only the lab environment.
4. Create one metric relabel rule that drops an intentionally generated debug metric.
5. Validate and reload the configuration.
6. Inspect active targets, dropped targets, labels and scrape metrics.

7. Break one port, observe failure, repair it and record recovery time.
8. Compare samples scraped before and after metric filtering. Validation Evidence

promtool validation output.

Active and dropped target evidence.

Before/after sample counts.



Final label contract.

Sanitized configuration diff and rollback result. Interview Questions and Model Answers
Q: What is the difference between relabel_configs and metric_relabel_configs?
A: Target relabeling operates on discovered target labels before scraping; metric relabeling operates on
scraped samples just before ingestion. Q: Why can honor_labels be risky?
A: It can allow target-provided labels to override server-side labels, potentially breaking ownership or
uniqueness conventions. Q: How do you debug a missing target?
A: Check discovery first, then relabeling and dropped targets, then final address/path/scheme, network
reachability, endpoint response and scrape logs. Chapter Summary

Discovery defines candidates; relabeling defines the final targets and labels.

Scrape intervals, timeouts and limits must be justified by measured reliability and cost needs.

Target and sample filtering require evidence because an incorrect rule can silently remove critical
telemetry.

Pushgateway Safety

Use it for service-level metrics from short-lived jobs when Prometheus cannot scrape the process during
execution.


Do not attach machine or instance lifecycle metrics that should disappear automatically with a target.

Choose a stable grouping key and delete pushed groups when they are no longer valid.

Export completion time, success state, duration and processed work rather than every internal event.

Monitor the Pushgateway itself and define stale-metric detection. Production Readiness Checklist

Run exporters with least privilege and only required collectors or queries.

Bind endpoints to approved networks and add TLS/authentication at an appropriate layer.

Set collection timeouts below the Prometheus scrape timeout.

Expose exporter process, scrape and collection-error metrics.

Normalize noisy filesystem, device, interface and mount labels.

Document credential rotation and failure behavior for third-party exporters.

Define cleanup ownership for Pushgateway groups. Troubleshooting Matrix

2. Write CPU, memory, disk-space and network-throughput queries.

Q: What is the difference between white-box and black-box monitoring?
A: White-box monitoring observes internal state exposed by the service; black-box monitoring tests externally
visible behavior from a probe location. Q: Why should Pushgateway not replace scraping for long-running services?

A: Pushed series are not automatically tied to process lifecycle, so stale metrics can remain and target health
semantics are lost. Q: What should a custom exporter expose about itself?
A: Collection duration, errors, last successful collection, process metrics, build information and bounded details
about backend status. Chapter Summary

Prefer direct instrumentation for owned applications and exporters for external systems or protocol probes.

Exporter health and probe target health are separate signals.

Pushgateway use requires strict workload selection, grouping and cleanup discipline.

Q: What is the purpose of Alertmanager grouping?
A: It combines related alert instances into a notification that reflects one operational event, reducing
notification storms while preserving needed scope. Q: What is the difference between inhibition and a silence?
A: Inhibition is automatic suppression based on another active alert and equal labels; a silence is a time-
bounded matcher created for a known maintenance or exception. Q: Why send alerts to all Alertmanager replicas?
A: It avoids making a load balancer a single selection point and allows the Alertmanager cluster to deduplicate
and coordinate notifications. Chapter Summary

Alertmanager is the notification policy layer: grouping, routing, inhibition, silencing and receiver delivery.

Configuration must be validated and tested with real label sets and synthetic receivers.

High availability requires peer health, direct delivery to replicas and failure testing.

Q: How would you prove a Prometheus platform is production-ready?
A: By validating configuration and rule semantics, measuring capacity and cardinality, monitoring the platform
itself, testing target/rule/notification paths, performing component-failure and rollback drills, and documenting
ownership and runbooks.

ownership and runbooks. Q: What is the most common root cause of Prometheus cost and performance problems?
A: Uncontrolled time-series cardinality, often caused by unbounded or multiplicative labels, combined with
expensive queries and unsuitable retention. Q: How do HA Prometheus and HA Alertmanager differ?
A: Prometheus replicas independently scrape and evaluate rules; Alertmanager peers coordinate state and
deduplicate notifications. Neither replaces a durability or global-query design. Chapter Summary
